source_refs.note: Practice MCQs written from Chapter 13 (PDF 291-304, printed 291-304); not printed in the book. Based on the chapter's text, tables, boxes and worked examples (numericals with changed values); none repeats the chapter exercise. Drafts needing academic review.

blocks.text: Practice MCQs for the whole of Chapter 13 (Halogens), arranged by the chapter's sections. Each question has one correct answer with a short explanation; numerical questions show the working.

blocks.prompt: 1 The halogens are the elements of:
blocks.explanation: Elements of Group 17 or VIIA of the periodic table are termed halogens (Introduction).

book_ref.quote: Elements present in Group 17 or VIIA of the periodic table are termed as halogens

blocks.prompt: 2 Which two members of the halogen family are very rare and radioactive?
blocks.explanation: The first four halogens are the common ones; astatine (At) and tennessine (Ts) are very rare and radioactive (Introduction).

book_ref.quote: astatine (At) and tennessine (Ts) are very rare and radioactive elements

blocks.prompt: 3 In the gas, liquid and solid phases, the halogens exist as:
blocks.explanation: Halogens exist as diatomic molecules in all phases (gas, liquid or solid) (Introduction).

book_ref.quote: Halogens exist as diatomic molecules in all phases (gas, liquid or solid)

blocks.prompt: 4 At room temperature bromine is a:
blocks.explanation: Bromine (Br₂) is a volatile liquid of reddish-brown colour at room temperature with corrosive, toxic fumes (Introduction).

book_ref.quote: Bromine (Br₂) is a volatile liquid of reddish-brown colour at room temperature

blocks.prompt: 5 On warming, solid iodine changes directly into a:
blocks.explanation: Iodine is a shiny greyish black solid that sublimes directly from solid to a violet vapour (Introduction).

book_ref.quote: It sublimes directly from solid to a violet vapor

blocks.prompt: 6 The colour of the halogens from chlorine to iodine:
blocks.explanation: The colours of the halogens darken progressively from chlorine to iodine, because of changes in light absorption by electron transitions within the molecules (Introduction).

book_ref.quote: The colors of halogens (X₂) darken progressively from chlorine to iodine

blocks.prompt: 7 The trend of colour change from chlorine to iodine is due to:

options.text: increase in the number of atoms in each molecule
changes in absorption of light due to electron transitions within the molecules
reaction of the halogens with air

blocks.explanation: The colour trend is due to changes in the absorption of light as a result of electron transitions within the halogen molecules (Introduction).

book_ref.quote: due to changes in the absorption of light as a result of electron transitions

blocks.prompt: 8 The first halogen to be isolated and recognised as an element was:
blocks.explanation: The 'Did You Know!' box states that chlorine was the first halogen to be isolated and recognised as an element (Introduction).

book_ref.quote: The first halogen to be isolated and recognized as an element was chlorine

blocks.prompt: 9 The name 'halogen' comes from Greek words meaning:
blocks.explanation: Halogen comes from the Greek 'halos' (salt) and 'gen' (to make), i.e. salt maker (Introduction box).

book_ref.quote: meaning “salt”, and “gen”, meaning “to make.”

blocks.prompt: 10 According to Table 13.1, the outer shell electron configuration of bromine is:
blocks.explanation: Table 13.1 gives F 2s²2p⁵, Cl 3s²3p⁵, Br 4s²4p⁵ and I 5s²5p⁵; every halogen has seven outer electrons (Introduction).

book_ref.quote: Outer shell electron configuration

blocks.prompt: 11 Using the relative atomic masses in Table 13.1, the molar mass of an I₂ molecule is:
blocks.explanation: Relative atomic mass of iodine = 126.9, so I₂ = 2 × 126.9 = 253.8 g mol⁻¹ (Table 13.1).

book_ref.quote: Table 13.1 Atomic and Physical properties of the common halogens.

blocks.prompt: 12 Table 13.1 gives the solubility of bromine as 3.6 g per 100 g of water at 20 °C. The mass of bromine that dissolves in 250 g of water at 20 °C is:

book_ref.quote: Solubility/g per 100g of water at 20ºC

blocks.prompt: 13 From the melting and boiling points in Table 13.1, bromine stays a liquid over a temperature range of:
blocks.explanation: Bromine melts at -7 °C and boils at 59 °C, so it is a liquid over 59 - (-7) = 66 °C, and is a liquid at 20 °C (Table 13.1).

book_ref.quote: Physical state at of 20 ºC

blocks.text: 13.1 Volatility of chlorine, bromine and iodine

blocks.prompt: 14 At room temperature, which of chlorine, bromine and iodine is the most volatile and disperses quickly in the air?
blocks.explanation: Chlorine is a gas at room temperature (book correction: not a liquid), so it is the most volatile of the three (13.1).

book_ref.quote: At room temperature chlorine is a gas (bromine is the liquid and iodine a solid)

blocks.prompt: 15 Compared with chlorine and iodine, bromine is:

options.text: less volatile than chlorine but more volatile than iodine

blocks.explanation: Bromine being a liquid is less volatile than chlorine but more volatile than iodine (13.1).

book_ref.quote: Bromine being a liquid is less volatile than chlorine but more volatile than iodine.

blocks.prompt: 16 The decrease in volatility from chlorine to iodine is due to all of the following EXCEPT:

options.text: increase in size of the outer shell

blocks.explanation: The trend is due to increasing molecular mass, increasing size of outer shell and stronger London dispersion forces down the group; molecular mass increases, not decreases (13.1).

book_ref.quote: This trend is due to the increasing molecular mass, increase in size of outer shell and stronger intermolecular forces

blocks.prompt: 17 Bromine liquid evaporates easily at room temperature, giving off a vapour that is:

options.text: orange with a very strong, bad odour

blocks.explanation: Bromine evaporates easily emitting an orange vapour; it has a very strong and bad odour, hence the name from Greek 'bromos' = stench (13.1 box).

book_ref.quote: Bromine liquid evaporates easily at room temperatures emitting an orange vapor.

blocks.text: 13.2 Trend in volatility of the halogens

blocks.prompt: 18 The main intermolecular forces that decide the volatility of the halogens are:
blocks.explanation: Halogens are non-polar, so instantaneous dipole-induced dipole (id-id, London) forces determine their volatility (13.2).

book_ref.quote: Halogens are non-polar and instantaneous dipole-induced forces play a significant role

blocks.prompt: 19 Instantaneous dipole-induced dipole forces depend on:

options.text: only the colour of the molecule

blocks.explanation: These forces depend on molecular size, shape and polarizability; stronger forces mean lower volatility (13.2).

book_ref.quote: The forces depend on factors like molecular size, shape and polarizability

blocks.prompt: 20 A more volatile substance has:
blocks.explanation: Volatility is inversely related to boiling point; a more volatile substance has a lower boiling point (13.2).

book_ref.quote: Volatility is inversely related to the boiling point of a substance.

blocks.prompt: 21 According to Table 13.2, a large molecule of high polarizability has:

options.text: strong id-id forces, higher boiling point and lower volatility
weak id-id forces, lower boiling point and higher volatility
strong id-id forces and higher volatility
weak id-id forces and higher boiling point

blocks.explanation: Table 13.2: large size, high polarizability, strong id-id forces, higher boiling point, lower volatility (13.2).

book_ref.quote: Instantaneous dipole-induced dipole forces

blocks.prompt: 22 Stronger intermolecular forces give a higher boiling point because:

options.text: the covalent X-X bond must break
more energy is needed to separate the molecules from the liquid to the gas phase

blocks.explanation: Stronger intermolecular forces require more energy to separate molecules from the liquid phase to the gaseous phase (13.2).

book_ref.quote: Stronger intermolecular forces require more energy to separate the molecules

blocks.prompt: 23 Bromine is a liquid at room temperature while chlorine is a gas because bromine:

options.text: is smaller and has weaker forces
is bigger and has stronger intermolecular forces

blocks.explanation: Bromine is a liquid because its size is bigger and it has stronger intermolecular forces than fluorine and chlorine (13.2).

book_ref.quote: Bromine is a liquid as its size is bigger and it possesses stronger intermolecular forces

blocks.prompt: 24 Iodine is a solid at room temperature because it has:

options.text: the weakest id-id forces in the group
the smallest molecules in the group
the strongest id-id forces in the group

blocks.explanation: Iodine has the strongest intermolecular forces among the halogens, so it is a solid at room temperature (13.2).

book_ref.quote: Iodine has the strongest forces among the group, so it is in solid state at room temperature.

blocks.prompt: 25 Using Table 13.1, the difference between the boiling points of bromine and chlorine is:
blocks.explanation: Boiling points: Br₂ 59 °C, Cl₂ -35 °C; difference = 59 - (-35) = 94 °C; the bigger Br₂ has stronger London forces (13.2, Table 13.1).

book_ref.quote: Table 13.2 Effect of London forces on physical properties

blocks.text: 13.3 The bond strength of halogen molecules

blocks.prompt: 26 From chlorine to iodine the X-X bond strength decreases because:

options.text: atomic size increases, giving longer and weaker bonds
the number of lone pairs decreases

blocks.explanation: Atomic size increases down the group, so bond lengths become longer and bonds weaker (13.3).

book_ref.quote: increase in the atomic size down the group which results in longer bond lengths and weaker bonds

blocks.prompt: 27 The F-F bond is weaker than expected because:

options.text: the small F atoms bring their lone pairs close, causing strong electron-electron repulsion

blocks.explanation: Fluorine atoms are very small, so lone pairs on the two atoms repel strongly, weakening the bond despite fluorine's high electronegativity (13.3, Fig. 13.1).

book_ref.quote: However, fluorine is an exception in this group.

blocks.prompt: 28 According to Table 13.3, the correct order of bond energy is:
blocks.explanation: Bond energies: Cl₂ 243, Br₂ 193, F₂ 156, I₂ 151 kJ mol⁻¹, so Cl₂ > Br₂ > F₂ > I₂ (Table 13.3).

book_ref.quote: Table 13.3 Bond energies of halogen molecules

blocks.prompt: 29 From Table 13.3, by how much is the bond energy of Cl₂ greater than that of F₂?
blocks.explanation: Cl₂ 243 - F₂ 156 = 87 kJ mol⁻¹ (Table 13.3).

book_ref.quote: Moving from top to bottom in group 17, the bond energy of halogens decreases gradually from chlorine to iodine.

blocks.prompt: 30 Each fluorine atom in the F₂ molecule (Fig. 13.1) carries how many lone pairs of electrons?
blocks.explanation: Fluorine has seven outer electrons (2s²2p⁵); one is used in the F-F bond and six remain as three lone pairs, which repel each other (13.3, Fig. 13.1).

book_ref.quote: F2 molecule with lone pairs of electrons

blocks.text: 13.4 Relative reactivities of the halogens as oxidising agents

blocks.prompt: 31 When halogens form ionic compounds with metals, they:

options.text: lose electrons and become positive ions
gain electrons and become negative halide ions

blocks.explanation: On forming ionic compounds with metals the halogens gain electrons and become negative halide ions, e.g. 2Na + Cl₂ → 2NaCl; they act as oxidizing agents (13.4).

book_ref.quote: the halogens gain electrons and are converted to negative halide ions

blocks.prompt: 32 The weakest oxidizing agent among the halogens F₂, Cl₂, Br₂ and I₂ is:
blocks.explanation: Oxidizing power decreases down the group: F₂ > Cl₂ > Br₂ > I₂; iodine is the least (13.4).

book_ref.quote: Fluorine has the highest oxidizing power and iodine the least.

blocks.prompt: 33 Chlorine water is added to potassium iodide solution. Which change takes place?

options.text: I⁻ is oxidized to I₂ and Cl₂ is reduced to Cl⁻

blocks.explanation: Chlorine can oxidize and displace Br⁻ and I⁻: Cl₂ + 2I⁻ → 2Cl⁻ + I₂ (13.4).

book_ref.quote: Similarly, chlorine can oxidize and displace Br⁻ and I⁻.

blocks.prompt: 34 Which mixture shows NO reaction?
blocks.explanation: A halogen displaces only the halide ions below it; iodine cannot oxidize any halide ion, so I₂ + Br⁻ gives no reaction (13.4).

book_ref.quote: Iodine cannot oxidize any halide ion.

blocks.prompt: 35 Bromine can oxidize and displace:
blocks.explanation: Bromine can oxidize and displace only I⁻, which lies below it (13.4).

book_ref.quote: Bromine can oxidize and displace I⁻.

blocks.prompt: 36 In the balanced equation for fluorine displacing chloride ions, one F₂ molecule reacts with:

options.text: one Cl⁻ ion, giving one F⁻ ion
two Cl⁻ ions, giving two F⁻ ions and one Cl₂
four Cl⁻ ions, giving two Cl₂
one Cl⁻ ion, giving one Cl₂

blocks.explanation: Balanced (book correction): F₂(g) + 2Cl⁻(aq) → 2F⁻(aq) + Cl₂(g); one F₂ gives two fluoride ions (13.4).

book_ref.quote: The balanced equations are F₂(g) + 2Cl¹⁻(aq) → 2F¹⁻(aq) + Cl₂(g)

blocks.prompt: 37 The standard electrode potentials E° (X₂/X⁻) of the halogens from fluorine to iodine:

options.text: become less positive, showing decreasing oxidizing power

blocks.explanation: E° values become less positive from F₂ (+2.87 V) to I₂ (+0.54 V), reflecting decreasing oxidizing power (13.4, Table 13.4).

book_ref.quote: become less positive from fluorine to iodine

blocks.prompt: 38 Using Table 13.4, the difference between the E° values of Cl₂ and Br₂ is:
blocks.explanation: E°(Cl₂) = +1.36 V, E°(Br₂) = +1.07 V; difference = 1.36 - 1.07 = 0.29 V; chlorine is the stronger oxidizing agent (Table 13.4).

book_ref.quote: Table 13.4 Standard electrode potential E° (X₂/X⁻)

blocks.prompt: 39 A halogen will have high oxidizing power if it has:

options.text: high dissociation energy and low electron affinity
low dissociation energy, high electron affinity and high hydration energy of its ions
low electron affinity and low hydration energy
high dissociation energy and low hydration energy

blocks.explanation: A halogen with low energy of dissociation, high electron affinity and higher hydration energy of its ions has high oxidizing power (13.4).

book_ref.quote: A halogen having low energy of dissociation, high electron affinity and higher hydration energy of its ions, will have a high oxidizing power.

blocks.prompt: 40 The heat of vaporization is listed as a factor in the oxidizing power of only:
blocks.explanation: The factors are dissociation energy, electron affinity, hydration energy and heats of vaporization (for Br₂ and I₂), which are not gases at room temperature (13.4).

book_ref.quote: energy of dissociation, electron affinity of atoms, hydration energies of ions, and heats of vaporization

blocks.text: 13.5 Reactions of the halogens with hydrogen

blocks.prompt: 41 Hydrogen halides are:

options.text: colourless gases that dissolve in water to form hydrohalic acids
white solids that form bases in water

blocks.explanation: Hydrogen halides are colourless gases that dissolve in water to form hydrohalic acids (13.5).

book_ref.quote: Hydrogen halides are colourless gases that dissolve in water to form hydrohalic acid.

blocks.prompt: 42 Fluorine reacts with hydrogen:

options.text: only on heating with a catalyst
explosively, even at low temperature and in the dark

blocks.explanation: At low temperature and in the dark, fluorine reacts explosively with hydrogen: H₂ + F₂ → 2HF (13.5).

book_ref.quote: At low temperature and in the dark, fluorine reacts explosively with hydrogen.

blocks.prompt: 43 The condition needed for chlorine to react readily with hydrogen is:
blocks.explanation: In the presence of UV light or a spark, chlorine reacts readily with hydrogen giving colourless HCl gas (13.5).

book_ref.quote: In the presence of UV light or a spark, chlorine reacts readily with hydrogen

blocks.prompt: 44 Bromine reacts with hydrogen to form HBr:

options.text: upon heating, in an exothermic reaction
only in the presence of a spark

blocks.explanation: HBr is produced when bromine reacts with hydrogen upon heating; the reaction is exothermic (13.5).

book_ref.quote: Hydrogen bromide (HBr) gas is produced when bromine reacts with the hydrogen upon heating.

blocks.prompt: 45 The reaction H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g) is:

options.text: fast and irreversible in UV light
complete at room temperature without a catalyst
reversible and very slow, needing high temperature and a catalyst

blocks.explanation: Iodine reacts with hydrogen at high temperature with a catalyst; the reaction is reversible and occurs very slowly (13.5).

book_ref.quote: This is a reversible reaction and occurs very slowly.

blocks.prompt: 46 Using Table 13.1 and H = 1, the mass of HCl formed when 7.1 g of chlorine reacts completely with hydrogen (H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl) is:

book_ref.quote: When halogen elements react with hydrogen, they produce hydrogen halides.

blocks.prompt: 47 The halogen that needs the most severe conditions (high temperature and a catalyst) to react with hydrogen is:
blocks.explanation: Reactivity with hydrogen decreases from fluorine to iodine; iodine needs high temperature and a catalyst (13.5).

book_ref.quote: When we move down the group from fluorine to iodine, the reactivity of halogens with hydrogen decreases.

blocks.text: 13.6 Relative thermal stabilities of hydrogen halides in terms of their bond strength

blocks.prompt: 48 The order of thermal stability of the hydrogen halides is:
blocks.explanation: Thermal stability decreases down the group with falling bond dissociation energy: HF > HCl > HBr > HI (13.6).

book_ref.quote: Hydrogen fluoride (HF) is the most thermally stable hydrogen halide.

blocks.prompt: 49 The H-F bond is very strong because:

options.text: fluorine has a large atomic radius
fluorine's high electronegativity and small radius give strong orbital overlap

blocks.explanation: Due to the high electronegativity and small atomic radius of fluorine, strong overlap of orbitals produces a very strong H-F bond (13.6).

book_ref.quote: a strong overlap of orbitals produces a very strong H-F bond

blocks.prompt: 50 From Table 13.5, the difference between the bond dissociation energies of H-F and H-I is:
blocks.explanation: H-F 569 - H-I 299 = 270 kJ mol⁻¹ (Table 13.5).

book_ref.quote: Table 13.5 Bond dissociation energy of H-X bonds

blocks.prompt: 51 The bond dissociation energy of H-Br given in the chapter is:
blocks.explanation: H-Br: 366 kJ mol⁻¹; weaker than H-F and H-Cl because of the larger atomic radius of bromine and reduced orbital overlap (13.6).

book_ref.quote: Its bond dissociation energy is 366 kJ/mol.

blocks.prompt: 52 HI is the least thermally stable hydrogen halide because:

options.text: iodine is the most electronegative halogen
HI has the strongest H-X bond
the very large iodine atom gives poor orbital overlap and the weakest H-X bond

blocks.explanation: The very large atomic radius of iodine leads to poor orbital overlap, so the H-I bond is the weakest (299 kJ mol⁻¹) (13.6).

book_ref.quote: Atomic radius of iodine is very large leading to poor orbital overlap

blocks.prompt: 53 From Table 13.5, how much more energy is needed to break one mole of H-Cl bonds than one mole of H-Br bonds?
blocks.explanation: 431 - 366 = 65 kJ per mole; HCl is more thermally stable than HBr (13.6).

book_ref.quote: Its bond dissociation energy is 431 KJ/mol.

blocks.text: 13.7 Relative reactivity of halide ions as reducing agents

blocks.prompt: 54 The weakest reducing agent among the halide ions is:
blocks.explanation: Reducing power: I⁻ > Br⁻ > Cl⁻ > F⁻; fluoride is the weakest reducing agent (13.7).

book_ref.quote: Fluoride ion is the weakest reducing agent while iodide is the strongest reducing agent among the halides.

blocks.prompt: 55 The reducing ability of halide ions increases down the group mainly because:

options.text: electronegativity decreases and atomic radius increases
the ions gain more protons than electrons

blocks.explanation: Decreasing electronegativity and increasing atomic radius give lower charge density and easier electron donation (13.7).

book_ref.quote: decreasing electronegativity and increasing atomic radius down the group

blocks.prompt: 56 The fluoride ion has little tendency to lose an electron because of its:

options.text: large size and low charge density
small size and high charge density
weak hold on its extra electron

blocks.explanation: The small fluoride ion has a high charge density and fluorine holds its extra electron strongly, so F⁻ hardly donates electrons (13.7).

book_ref.quote: The small size of fluoride ion results in a high charge density

blocks.prompt: 57 Compared with the chloride ion, the bromide ion is:

options.text: a stronger reducing agent with larger radius and lower charge density
a weaker reducing agent with higher charge density

blocks.explanation: Br⁻ has a larger ionic radius and lower charge density, so it loses an electron more easily than Cl⁻ (13.7).

book_ref.quote: Bromide ion (Br⁻) has a larger ionic radius and lower charge density

blocks.prompt: 58 Which statement about the chloride ion as a reducing agent is correct?

options.text: it is the strongest halide reducing agent
it is stronger than F⁻ but weaker than Br⁻ and I⁻
it is stronger than I⁻ but weaker than Br⁻

blocks.explanation: Cl⁻ is a stronger reducing agent than fluoride but still weaker than bromide and iodide, because of its larger size and lower electronegativity than fluoride (13.7).

book_ref.quote: Chloride ion (Cl⁻) is a stronger reducing agent than fluoride but still weaker than bromide and iodide.

blocks.text: 13.8 Reactions of halides with aqueous silver ion followed by aqueous ammonia

blocks.prompt: 59 The reagent added first to identify halide ions in the silver nitrate test is:
blocks.explanation: Insoluble silver halides form when halide ions react with aqueous AgNO₃; this is used in qualitative analysis (13.8.1).

book_ref.quote: Insoluble silver halides (AgX) are formed when halide ions react with aqueous silver nitrate (AgNO₃).

blocks.prompt: 60 The correct general ionic equation for the precipitation of a silver halide is:
blocks.explanation: Book correction: the silver ion is Ag⁺ and one Ag⁺ with one X⁻ gives one AgX: X⁻(aq) + Ag⁺(aq) → AgX(s) (13.8.1).

book_ref.quote: The correct equation is X¹⁻(aq) + Ag¹⁺(aq) → AgX(s).

blocks.prompt: 61 No visible change occurs when aqueous silver nitrate is added to a fluoride solution because:

options.text: fluoride ions do not exist in water
silver fluoride is soluble in water
silver fluoride dissolves only in ammonia

blocks.explanation: Silver fluoride is soluble in water, so F⁻ gives no precipitate with Ag⁺ (13.8.1).

book_ref.quote: As silver fluoride is soluble in water, Fluoride (F⁻) does not form precipitate as silver fluoride.

blocks.prompt: 62 The colour of the silver chloride precipitate is:
blocks.explanation: Ag⁺ + Cl⁻ gives a white precipitate of AgCl, soluble in dilute ammonia (13.8.1).

book_ref.quote: a white precipitate of silver chloride forms, which is soluble in dilute ammonia

blocks.prompt: 63 Aqueous silver ions give a cream-coloured precipitate with:
blocks.explanation: Ag⁺ with Br⁻ forms a cream-coloured precipitate of AgBr (13.8.1, Fig. 13.2).

book_ref.quote: a cream-coloured precipitate of silver bromide forms

blocks.prompt: 64 In Fig. 13.2, the silver halide precipitates from left to right are:
blocks.explanation: Fig. 13.2 shows silver chloride (left), silver bromide (middle) and silver iodide (right): white, cream and yellow (13.8.1).

book_ref.quote: Colours of the silver halide precipitates

blocks.prompt: 65 Using Ag = 108 and Table 13.1 (Na = 23 given), the mass of AgCl precipitated when 1.17 g of NaCl reacts completely with excess AgNO₃ is:
blocks.explanation: Moles NaCl = 1.17/58.5 = 0.02 mol = moles AgCl (Ag⁺ + Cl⁻ → AgCl); mass = 0.02 × 143.5 = 2.87 g (13.8.1).

book_ref.quote: This type of reactions is used to identify halide ions and is called silver nitrate test.

blocks.prompt: 66 Silver chloride dissolves in dilute ammonia forming the complex ion:
blocks.explanation: AgCl(s) + 2NH₃(aq) → [Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq); the diamminesilver(I) complex gives a colourless solution (13.8.2).

book_ref.quote: Silver chloride dissolves in dilute ammonia to form diamminesilver(1) complex.

blocks.prompt: 67 The number of NH₃ molecules that combine with one AgBr when it dissolves in concentrated ammonia is:
blocks.explanation: AgBr(s) + 2NH₃(aq) → [Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺(aq) + Br⁻(aq): two NH₃ per AgBr (13.8.2).

book_ref.quote: The cream-coloured precipitate of AgBr dissolves in concentrated ammonia

blocks.prompt: 68 The yellow precipitate of silver iodide in ammonia solution:

options.text: does not dissolve in dilute or concentrated ammonia

blocks.explanation: AgI does not dissolve in dilute or concentrated ammonia, so there is no change (13.8.2).

book_ref.quote: does not dissolve in both dilute and concentrated ammonia

blocks.prompt: 69 Which halide ion gives no precipitate with Ag⁺(aq) and so shows no reaction with aqueous ammonia either?
blocks.explanation: AgF is soluble in water so no precipitate forms, and ammonia has no effect (13.8.2, Table 13.6).

book_ref.quote: AgF is soluble in water so it does not form precipitate, so ammonia has no effect.

blocks.prompt: 70 An unknown solution gives a precipitate with Ag⁺(aq) that dissolves in dilute ammonia. The halide ion present is:
blocks.explanation: Table 13.6: only the white AgCl precipitate is soluble in dilute aqueous NH₃; AgBr needs concentrated NH₃ and AgI is insoluble (13.8.2).

book_ref.quote: Table 13.6 Action of Ag⁺ followed by ammonia on silver halides

blocks.prompt: 71 A precipitate with Ag⁺(aq) that is insoluble in aqueous ammonia shows the presence of:
blocks.explanation: Table 13.6: I⁻ gives a pale yellow precipitate of AgI, insoluble in aqueous NH₃ (13.8.2).

book_ref.quote: Pale yellow precipitate (AgI)

blocks.text: 13.9 Reactions of halides (X-) with concentrated sulfuric acid

blocks.prompt: 72 When concentrated H₂SO₄ reacts with NaF, the HF formed does not react further because HF is:
blocks.explanation: NaF + H₂SO₄ → NaHSO₄ + HF; HF is a weak reducing agent, so it does not react with H₂SO₄ further (13.9).

book_ref.quote: HF is a weak reducing agent, therefore, it does not react with H₂SO₄ further.

blocks.prompt: 73 When concentrated sulfuric acid is added to sodium bromide, the observations are:

options.text: purple fumes and the smell of H₂S
steamy HBr fumes, brown Br₂ fumes and the smell of SO₂

blocks.explanation: With Br⁻: steamy fumes of HBr, brown fumes of Br₂ and the smell of SO₂; it is a redox reaction (13.9).

book_ref.quote: steamy fumes of hydrogen bromide (HBr) gas and brown fumes of bromine (Br₂) are produced along with the smell of sulfur dioxide (SO₂)

blocks.prompt: 74 In the balanced equation 2HBr(g) + H₂SO₄(l) → Br₂(g) + SO₂(g) + 2H₂O(l), the oxidation state of sulfur changes from:
blocks.explanation: S in H₂SO₄ is +6 and in SO₂ is +4; HBr reduces sulfuric acid to SO₂ and is oxidized to Br₂ (13.9, book correction).

book_ref.quote: so it is 2HBr(g) + H₂SO₄(l) → Br₂(g) + SO₂(g) + 2H₂O(l)

blocks.prompt: 75 Hydrogen iodide reduces concentrated sulfuric acid to:
blocks.explanation: HI is a strong reducing agent; it reduces H₂SO₄ to H₂S and is itself oxidized to I₂ (13.9).

book_ref.quote: It reduces H₂SO₄ to H₂S and is itself oxidized to I₂.

blocks.prompt: 76 In the reaction 8HI(g) + H₂SO₄(l) → 4I₂(s) + H₂S(g) + 4H₂O(l), the oxidation state of sulfur falls by:
blocks.explanation: S goes from +6 in H₂SO₄ to -2 in H₂S, a fall of 8, matched by 8 I⁻ each losing one electron (13.9).

book_ref.quote: 8HI(g) + H₂SO₄(l) → 4I₂(s) + H₂S(g) + 4H₂O(l)

blocks.prompt: 77 Purple fumes and the smell of H₂S are observed when concentrated sulfuric acid reacts with:
blocks.explanation: With NaI: fumes of HI, purple fumes of iodine and the smell of H₂S (13.9).

book_ref.quote: purple fumes of solid iodine I₂ and smell of H₂S gas produced

blocks.prompt: 78 The reactions of concentrated H₂SO₄ with NaF and with NaCl are similar because in both:

options.text: only the hydrogen halide and NaHSO₄ form; there is no redox step

blocks.explanation: NaF and NaCl give only HF or HCl fumes with NaHSO₄; these hydrogen halides are too weak as reducing agents to reduce the acid (13.9).

book_ref.quote: When concentrated sulfuric acid reacts with sodium chloride, fumes of hydrogen chloride gas are produced.

blocks.prompt: 79 In the reaction of HBr with concentrated sulfuric acid, HBr acts as:

options.text: a reducing agent, itself oxidized to Br₂

blocks.explanation: HBr reduces sulfuric acid to SO₂ and is itself oxidized to bromine (13.9).

book_ref.quote: Hydrogen bromide acts as a reducing agent by reducing sulfuric acid to sulfur dioxide and is self-oxidized to bromine.

blocks.text: 13.10 Reactions of chlorine with cold and hot aqueous sodium hydroxide

blocks.prompt: 80 A reaction in which the same element is oxidized and reduced at the same time is called a:
blocks.explanation: Reactions in which a single element undergoes both oxidation and reduction simultaneously are disproportionation reactions (13.10).

book_ref.quote: Those reactions in which a single element undergoes both oxidation and reduction simultaneously are known as disproportionation reactions.

blocks.prompt: 81 With cold aqueous sodium hydroxide, chlorine forms:
blocks.explanation: Cl₂(g) + 2NaOH(aq) → NaCl(aq) + NaClO(aq) + H₂O(l) with cold NaOH (13.10.1).

book_ref.quote: forming sodium chloride (NaCl) and sodium chlorate (I) (NaClO)

blocks.prompt: 82 The older name of sodium chlorate(I), NaClO, is:
blocks.explanation: Sodium chlorate (I) was previously called sodium hypochlorite (13.10.1, Keep in Mind).

book_ref.quote: Sodium chlorate (I) is previously called sodium hypochlorite.

blocks.prompt: 83 In the reaction of chlorine with cold NaOH, chlorine in NaCl has been:
blocks.explanation: Book correction: chlorine in NaCl is -1, so it is reduced from 0 to -1 (13.10.1).

book_ref.quote: so it is reduced from 0 to -1

blocks.prompt: 84 The oxidation state of chlorine in sodium chlorate(I) is:
blocks.explanation: Chlorine is oxidized from 0 in Cl₂ to +1 in NaOCl (13.10.1).

book_ref.quote: Chlorine in Cl₂ is oxidized from 0 to +1 in NaOCl.

blocks.prompt: 85 Using Table 13.1 and Na = 23, O = 16, H = 1, the mass of NaClO formed when 14.2 g of chlorine reacts with excess cold aqueous NaOH is:
blocks.explanation: Cl₂ + 2NaOH → NaCl + NaClO + H₂O. Moles Cl₂ = 14.2/71.0 = 0.2 mol = moles NaClO; mass = 0.2 × 74.5 = 14.9 g (13.10.1).

book_ref.quote: Chlorine undergoes disproportion when it reacts with cold aqueous sodium hydroxide

blocks.prompt: 86 With hot aqueous sodium hydroxide, the chlorine-containing products are:
blocks.explanation: Hot NaOH gives sodium chloride and sodium chlorate (V), NaClO₃ (13.10.2).

book_ref.quote: it forms sodium chloride (NaCl) and sodium chlorate (V) (NaClO₃)

blocks.prompt: 87 In the balanced equation for chlorine with hot NaOH, the coefficient of NaCl is:
blocks.explanation: Book correction: 3Cl₂ + 6NaOH → 5NaCl + NaClO₃ + 3H₂O (6 Cl and 6 Na on each side) (13.10.2).

book_ref.quote: The balanced equation is 3Cl₂(g) + 6NaOH(aq) → 5NaCl(aq) + NaClO₃(aq) + 3H₂O(l)

blocks.prompt: 88 In the reaction of chlorine with hot NaOH, the ratio of chlorine atoms reduced to chlorine atoms oxidized is:
blocks.explanation: Of six Cl atoms, five are reduced to -1 (NaCl) and one is oxidized to +5 (NaClO₃): 5 : 1; electrons 5 × 1 = 1 × 5 (13.10.2).

book_ref.quote: five Cl atoms are reduced to -1 and one is oxidised to +5

blocks.prompt: 89 Using Table 13.1 and Na = 23, O = 16, the mass of NaClO₃ formed from 21.3 g of chlorine with excess hot aqueous NaOH is:
blocks.explanation: Moles Cl₂ = 21.3/71.0 = 0.3 mol; NaClO₃ = 0.3/3 = 0.1 mol; mass = 0.1 × 106.5 = 10.65 g (13.10.2, balanced equation).

book_ref.quote: Chlorine is oxidized from 0 to +5 in NaClO₃.

blocks.prompt: 90 The different products of chlorine with cold and with hot NaOH show that:

options.text: the temperature of the reaction influences the products formed
temperature has no effect on the products
chlorine is only reduced in hot NaOH
chlorine is only oxidized in cold NaOH

blocks.explanation: This disproportionation shows how temperature influences the products, demonstrating the versatility of chlorine in redox reactions (13.10.2).

book_ref.quote: how the temperature of the reaction influences the products formed

blocks.text: 13.11 Use of chlorine in water purification

blocks.prompt: 91 Chlorine can be used to purify drinking water because, in small quantities, it is:

options.text: harmful to humans but harmless to bacteria
harmless to both humans and bacteria
harmless to humans but poisonous to disease-causing bacteria

blocks.explanation: Chlorine gas is very poisonous, but in small quantities it is harmless to humans and poisonous to disease-causing bacteria (13.11).

book_ref.quote: in small quantities, they are harmless to humans but poisonous to the bacteria

blocks.prompt: 92 Swimming-pool water is chlorinated with slightly higher concentrations of chlorine because:

options.text: it is not used by people
it is likely to contain a higher concentration of bacteria

blocks.explanation: Swimming-pool water is likely to have a higher concentration of bacteria, so it is chlorinated slightly more (13.11).

book_ref.quote: because there is likely to be a higher concentration of bacteria in the water

blocks.prompt: 93 The primary active species that kill bacteria in chlorinated water are:
blocks.explanation: The primary active species are chloric (I) acid / hypochlorous acid (HOCl) and chlorate (I) / hypochlorite ions (OCl⁻) (13.11).

book_ref.quote: The primary active species are chloric (I) acid or hypochlorous acid (HOCl)

blocks.prompt: 94 When chlorine gas is added to water, it undergoes hydrolysis to give:
blocks.explanation: Cl₂(g) + H₂O(l) → HCl(aq) + HClO(aq): hydrochloric acid and chloric (I) acid (13.11.1).

book_ref.quote: it undergoes hydrolysis to form a mixture of hydrochloric acid (HCl) and chloric (I) acid (HClO)

blocks.prompt: 95 Chloric(I) acid, HOCl, in water:

options.text: is a weak acid that partially dissociates into H⁺ and OCl⁻
is a strong acid that fully ionizes

blocks.explanation: HOCl is a weak acid and partially dissociates in water to give H⁺ and the chlorate (I) ion OCl⁻ (13.11.1).

book_ref.quote: is a weak acid and partially dissociate in water

blocks.prompt: 96 In the reaction Cl₂ + H₂O → HCl + HClO, the oxidation states of chlorine in HCl and HClO are:
blocks.explanation: Cl is -1 in HCl and +1 in HClO; one Cl atom is reduced and one oxidized from 0 (13.11.1).

book_ref.quote: When chlorine gas (Cl₂) is added to water

blocks.prompt: 97 HOCl is a more effective disinfectant than OCl⁻ because:

options.text: being neutral, it penetrates the cell walls of micro-organisms easily

blocks.explanation: HOCl is neutral, which allows it to penetrate the cell walls of micro-organisms easily (13.11.2).

book_ref.quote: HOCl and OCl⁻ are effective disinfectants, but HOCl is more effective due to its neutral charge.

blocks.prompt: 98 HOCl and OCl⁻ kill micro-organisms by:

options.text: oxidizing proteins, lipids and enzymes, disrupting cell function

blocks.explanation: HOCl and OCl⁻ oxidize proteins and lipids and inactivate enzymes, disrupting cell function and causing cell death (13.11.2).

book_ref.quote: Essential cellular components such as proteins and lipids are oxidized by HOCl and OCl⁻

blocks.prompt: 99 Oxidation of nucleic acids (DNA and RNA) by HOCl and OCl⁻ mainly prevents bacteria from:
blocks.explanation: Nucleic acids oxidized by HOCl and OCl⁻ prevent bacteria from replicating and from vital cellular functions (13.11.2 box).

book_ref.quote: Nucleic acids (DNA and RNA) can be oxidized by HOCl and OCl⁻

blocks.prompt: 100 Disinfection of water by chlorine is most effective at a pH of about:
blocks.explanation: At pH around 6-7.5 HOCl predominates and disinfection is more effective; above 7.5 OCl⁻ predominates and is less effective (13.11.3).

book_ref.quote: At pH around 6-7.5, HOCl predominates and makes the disinfection process more effective.

blocks.prompt: 101 Which is NOT a factor affecting disinfection listed in the chapter?
blocks.explanation: The factors listed are pH, chlorine dose and contact time (13.11.3).

book_ref.quote: Contact time of water with chlorine must be long enough

blocks.prompt: 102 Regarding the chlorine dose, the chapter states that:

options.text: any trace of chlorine is enough
the higher the amount of chlorine, the more effective the disinfection

blocks.explanation: The higher the amount of chlorine, the more effective the disinfection; sufficient chlorine must give enough HOCl and OCl⁻ (13.11.3).

book_ref.quote: Sufficient chlorine must be added to get enough HOCl and OCl⁻ to kill bacteria.

blocks.prompt: 103 One advantage of chlorination stated in the chapter is that it is:

options.text: able to remove all dissolved salts
a relatively inexpensive method of water disinfection
a method that needs no contact time

blocks.explanation: Chlorination is a relatively inexpensive method of water disinfection (13.11).

book_ref.quote: Chlorination is a relatively inexpensive method of water disinfections.
